newsitem.title: INDIA: Marxist ally flays Indian government's policies.
newsitem.headline: Marxist ally flays Indian government's policies.

text.p: The Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), part of India's ruling coalition, attacked Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's economic policies on Tuesday but said it had no plans to withdraw its support.
The CPI-M, which has 32 seats in the 13-party United Front governing coalition but no ministerial posts, lambasted the government for welcoming foreign investors.

The party reacted strongly to the government's recent decision to allow foreign investors to take stakes of up to 74 percent in Indian firms in certain areas, and reaffirmed its opposition to efforts to privatise the insurance sector.
"Even the (domestic) industry has started opposing this," Surjeet said, referring to the move allowing the large foreign stakes. "We want a reversal of the policy."

The CPI-M also said it would observe a week-long protest against rising prices next month, but added it had no plans to cut its ties to the centre-left government, which was formed last June after inconclusive general elections.

"There is no question of dissociating at all," CPI-M general secretary Harkishan Singh Surjeet told a news conference in the capital, when asked if the party had considered withdrawing its support for the government
The CPI-M joined the other main communist party, the Communist Party of India, in speaking out against a possible increase in state-controlled petroleum prices.
The Communist Party of India is also a member of the United Front and has 12 seats and two cabinet ministers.

Analysts have said the strain of oil subsidies will sooner or later force Deve Gowda's government to raise domestic prices for the second time. But the prime minister said on Monday that the government had no intention at present to do so.
Surjeet also attacked rising grain prices, saying higher wheat and wheat flour costs were causing "immense hardships for people".

The United Front commands the support of 190 lawmakers, including independents, in the 545-member lower house of parliament. But the government's survival depends largely on the Congress party, which commands a further 140 lawmakers.
